target.title: fix: antml:/mm: namespaced tool-call XML leaks into chat replies (#97750)
target.body:
Closes #97750

## What Problem This Solves

Some deployments serve a Claude/MiniMax model through a proxy that intermittently degrades a native `tool_use` block into plain text. In that degraded case the tool call arrives as the namespaced/bare XML attribute dialect — `<invoke name="tool"><parameter name="x">v</parameter></invoke>`, optionally wrapped in `<function_calls>...</function_calls>` and optionally prefixed with `antml:` or `mm:`.

On current `main` two gaps remained:

1. The visible-text sanitizer recognized the `antml:` prefix but not the `mm:` prefix, so a degraded `mm:invoke` block leaked verbatim into the user-visible reply.
2. The persist-path stripper (`packages/tool-call-repair` `stripPlainTextToolCallBlocks`) did not recognize the attribute-dialect invoke at all, so an unfenced standalone degraded invoke block was written into the durable `done.message` instead of being scrubbed.

## Why This Change Was Made

The degraded tool call should never reach the user, and it must not be persisted into session state either — but a legitimate code example of the same markup (inside a fenced or inline code span) must be preserved, not deleted. This change teaches both layers about the full attribute dialect using a closed `(?:antml:|mm:)?` namespace allow-list, so arbitrary `ns:` tokens in prose are never matched.

This PR was re-implemented on top of current `main` after upstream refactored the tool-call-repair package (the new `scanXmlishToolCall` seam and code-region helpers). The change is scoped to the net delta that still reproduces on `main`:

- **Visible text** (`assistant-visible-text.ts`): mirror the existing `antml:` handling for the `mm:` namespace in the tag-name scan, quick-check, and payload-start patterns. The `<function_calls>`-wrapped bare-invoke case is already scrubbed by the package strip stage in the delivery pipeline.
- **Persist path** (`packages/tool-call-repair`): a dedicated linear scanner recognizes a complete standalone invoke block (bare/`antml:`/`mm:`, `<function_calls>` wrapper, self-closing, and zero-parameter forms). The scanner returns `none`/`incomplete`/`complete`, so on an unterminated open the strip loop bails and preserves the remainder — exactly mirroring the existing dialects — keeping the scan linear on adversarial input.
- **Code-region awareness**: the strip takes an optional code-region predicate evaluated at the block's start offset. Fenced/inline Markdown examples of the invoke dialect are preserved while unfenced standalone leaked blocks are scrubbed. Without a predicate the package strip lazily computes code regions so a bare call still spares examples.
- **Plugin SDK contract preserved**: the exported `stripPlainTextToolCallBlocks` stays strict by default (it forces a scrub of every region, even inside code, for untrusted callers), with code-aware behavior available only via the explicit `{ preserveCodeRegions: true }` opt-in.
- **Layering**: `findCodeRegions`/`isInsideCode`/`CodeRegion` were moved into `normalization-core` (the package's only dependency) so `tool-call-repair` can share one implementation without importing app source; `src/shared/text/code-regions.ts` re-exports them so existing callers are unaffected.

Non-goals/boundaries: the native Anthropic/DSML transports are untouched; no runtime fallback execution from sanitized text is introduced; the equals dialect (`<function=...>`/`<parameter=...>`), bracket, and Harmony paths are unchanged; the invoke dialect is recognized only by the strip/sanitize paths (never promoted to an executable call and never wired into the stream-buffering scanner).

## User Impact

Users on proxied Claude/MiniMax routes no longer see raw namespaced/bare `invoke` tool-call XML in their replies, and the leaked block is no longer written into the persisted message (no session-state content loss). Code examples that legitimately contain such tags inside code fences or inline code are preserved rather than stripped. A resolved-review audit also removed an O(n²) worst case on the persist strip path, so adversarial degraded text cannot cause pathological CPU use.

## Evidence

Focused regression tests were added at the layers that own the contract:
- `packages/tool-call-repair/src/payload.test.ts`: invoke-dialect variants (bare/`antml:`/`mm:`, `function_calls` wrapper, self-closing, zero-param), code-region preservation vs. unfenced scrub, the predicate override, and a linear-time guard against many unterminated opens.
- `src/plugin-sdk/tool-payload.test.ts`: the `preserveCodeRegions` opt-in and strict default.
- `src/shared/text/assistant-visible-text.test.ts`: the `mm:invoke`/`mm:parameter` visible-text case (parallel to the existing `antml:` case), alongside existing standalone-vs-inline `function_calls` delivery-path coverage.

Real-behavior proof (before = current `main`, after = this branch), driving the actual `sanitizeAssistantVisibleText` and `stripPlainTextToolCallBlocks` on the leak shapes:

```
=== BEFORE (main) ===
A2 mm-visible       => "Working on it.\n<mm:invoke name=\"get_weather\">\n<mm:parameter name=\"city\">Paris</mm:parameter>\n</mm:invoke>"
A3 bare-fc-visible  => "Done.\n<function_calls>\n<invoke name=\"get_weather\">\n<parameter name=\"city\">Paris</parameter>\n</invoke>\n</function_calls>"
C1 persist-unfenced => "Here you go.\n<invoke name=\"get_weather\">\n<parameter name=\"city\">Paris</parameter>\n</invoke>"
B1 persist-fenced   => "...```xml\n<invoke ...>...\n```..."   (preserved)
B2 persist-inline   => "Use the `<invoke name=\"get_weather\">` opener to start."   (preserved)

=== AFTER (this branch) ===
A2 mm-visible       => "Working on it."
A3 bare-fc-visible  => "Done."
C1 persist-unfenced => "Here you go.\n"
B1 persist-fenced   => "...```xml\n<invoke ...>...\n```..."   (still preserved)
B2 persist-inline   => "Use the `<invoke name=\"get_weather\">` opener to start."   (still preserved)
```

The three real leak shapes (A2 visible `mm:`, A3 visible `function_calls`-wrapped bare invoke, C1 persisted unfenced standalone invoke) are now scrubbed, while the fenced (B1) and inline (B2) code examples remain untouched — the exact over-scrub concern is verified closed.

O(n²) audit fix: a resolved-review pass measured the persist strip degrading quadratically on adversarial input with many unterminated invoke opens (720 KB ≈ 977 ms, scaling to seconds for a few MB). Making the scanner bail on `incomplete` (mirroring the existing unterminated-candidate bail) brought the same 720 KB input to ≈ 0.8 ms and restored linear scaling; a regression test locks this.

Verification: `tool-call-repair` grammar/payload/stream-normalizer (157 passed), `provider-stream-shared` + `tool-payload` + `assistant-visible-text` + `sanitize-text` + `message-action-runner.send-validation` + `embedded-agent-utils` (all green), `tsgo:core` and `tsgo:core:test` exit 0, `plugin-sdk:api:check` and `plugin-sdk:surface:check` exit 0 (surface budget bumped by the one new `StripPlainTextToolCallOptions` type), oxfmt clean, `git diff --check` clean. Rebased onto current `main` (`9b823c61`).

Closes #104517

## What Problem This Solves

Resolves a problem where `openclaw attach --print-config` prints the full MCP
grant config, including `env.OPENCLAW_MCP_TOKEN` (a live, unrevoked bearer
credential), as plain JSON on stdout with no indication that it is sensitive.
A user copying that output into a log, chat transcript, screen share, or bug
report can leak the live token without realizing it.

## Why This Change Was Made

Added a clear warning printed to stderr immediately before the JSON payload is
printed to stdout. This keeps the warning visible to interactive users while
staying separable from stdout for any scripted consumers that pipe/parse the
JSON. This is the minimal fix addressing the issue's first suggested option
(a clear warning) without changing the printed config shape, redacting the
token (which would break the documented copy/launch workflow), or making a
larger product decision about a separate summary/redact mode.

## User Impact

Anyone running `attach --print-config` now sees an explicit stderr warning
that the printed env carries a live bearer token and should be treated as a
secret, reducing accidental credential leakage via copy/paste or logging.

## Evidence

- Added a regression test asserting an `ERR:`-prefixed stderr warning
  containing `OPENCLAW_MCP_TOKEN` and `secret` is emitted, and that it appears
  before the JSON payload in output order.
- Proved the regression: temporarily removed the new warning call and reran

target.title: fix(line): honor channelData.line.mediaKind on the reply-token path
target.body: Closes #106512 ## What Problem This Solves Fixes an issue where a LINE bot that replies to an inbound message with a video or audio attachment — and sets `channelData.line.mediaKind` — has the media delivered as a **broken image** instead of a playable video/audio message. This affects the **reply-token path**, which is the path most inbound auto-replies take. `docs/channels/line.md` states the media kind is taken from `channelData.line.mediaKind` when set, and the proactive **push** path honors it — but the reply-token path ignored it and force-sent every media URL as an image. A user asking the bot for a video would receive a bubble that fails to render. ## Why This Change Was Made The reply-token delivery in `auto-reply-delivery.ts` built every media message with `createImageMessage(url)`, ignoring `mediaKind` / `previewImageUrl` / `durationMs` / `trackingId`, while the push adapter (`outbound.ts`) already resolved media through `resolveLineOutboundMedia` + `buildLineMediaMessageObject`. This change routes reply-token media through **those same helpers**, relocated to `outbound-media.ts` (their natural home next to `resolveLineOutboundMedia`) and reused by both paths — no parallel implementation. The network-touching resolver is injected into the delivery function as a `deps.buildMediaMessage` field and wired in `monitor.ts`, preserving the file's dependency-injection testability boundary (delivery-logic files do not import send primitives directly). Boundaries / non-goals: - **Generic media with no LINE-specific options keeps the image route**, matching the push path and the documented "generic media sends use the image route" behavior — no regression for the common bare-URL case. - A media that **cannot be built** (e.g. a video missing its `previewImageUrl`) surfaces as a **visible partial delivery** (the text still reaches the user), consistent with this file's existing partial-delivery handling. - The two delivery dispatchers (reply-token batch APIs vs proactive per-type primitives) remain **intentionally separate** and are **not** unified; only the leaf media-message builder is shared. ## User Impact LINE bots that reply with `channelData.line.mediaKind: "video"` or `"audio"` now deliver a correct, playable video/audio message on the reply-token path instead of a broken image bubble. No change for text-only replies or for generic media sends without LINE-specific options. ## Evidence **Real inbound → reply-token path (redacted live transcript).** A real LINE message was sent to the test-channel bot; its **fresh reply token** drove the **actual** `deliverLineAutoReply` on this branch (real `send.ts` `replyMessageLine`, no mocks). A media-only reply is used so the video rides the reply token (a text chunk would consume it), exercising the exact changed reply-token wiring end-to-end. LINE accepted the reply: ```text [2026-07-13T17:56:43.917Z] harness listening on :3000 (ngrok -> /line) [2026-07-13T17:56:51.093Z] inbound message from U4aef1…2a replyToken=9f1eb3…22 [2026-07-13T17:56:51.094Z] agent reply payload: media-only, channelData.line.mediaKind="video" [2026-07-13T17:56:51.190Z] -> replyMessageLine (REPLY TOKEN 9f1eb3…22) types=["video"] [2026-07-13T17:56:51.505Z] deliverLineAutoReply result = {"status":"delivered","replyTokenUsed":true} ``` The `replyMessageLine (REPLY TOKEN …) types=["video"]` line is the point: driven by a real inbound message, the fixed reply-token path delivered a **video** via the reply token (`replyTokenUsed: true`) — not a downgraded image and not a push fallback. On current-main this same flow would have sent `type:"image"`. **Live LINE app — before/after (real test channel).** The exact message objects the reply path builds were delivered to a LINE chat (push and reply render identically in the client). Same source clip `https://download.samplelib.com/mp4/sample-5s.mp4` in both cases; LINE returned `HTTP 200` for both. **修復前 (Before):** the reply path forced `{"type":"image","originalContentUrl":".../sample-5s.mp4"}`. LINE cannot render an mp4 as an image, so the bubble is a **broken placeholder**: **修復後 (After):** the reply path honors `mediaKind="video"` and builds `{"type":"video","originalContentUrl":".../sample-5s.mp4","previewImageUrl":".../clouds.jpg"}` → a **playable video bubble**: **Deterministic repro against the real functions** (real `resolveLineOutboundMedia` + `buildLineMediaMessageObject`, the exact `monitor.ts` wiring), same input clip, three outcomes: ``` OLD reply path (hardcoded): always -> {"type":"image","originalContentUrl":".../clip.mp4","previewImageUrl":".../clip.mp4"} NEW — channelData.line = { mediaKind:"video", previewImageUrl } -> status: delivered reply message sent: {"type":"video","originalContentUrl":".../clip.mp4","previewImageUrl":".../preview.jpg"} NEW — generic media, no LINE options (parity) -> status: delivered reply message sent: {"type":"image","originalContentUrl":".../clip.mp4","previewImageUrl":".../clip.mp4"} ``` **Unit tests** — `pnpm exec vitest run --config test/vitest/vitest.extension-line.config.ts` on the touched suites (adds 3 reply-path media cases + a full `buildLineMediaMessageObject` / `hasLineSpecificMediaOptions` / `isLineUserTarget` suite): ``` Test Files 3 passed (3) Tests 44 passed (44) ``` **Red/green** — reverting only the reply-path media routing makes exactly the two new fix cases fail while the generic-image parity case stays green: ``` Tests 2 failed | 10 passed (12) × honors channelData.line.mediaKind ... expected "partial"/"video", received "delivered"/"image" ✓ keeps the image route for generic media without LINE-specific options ``` **Static checks** — `tsgo` extensions typecheck: pass · `pnpm lint:extensions` (oxlint): pass · `oxfmt --check` on touched files: pass. Branch **rebased onto current `main`** and re-verified. ---

target.title: fix(agents): preserve yielded subagent continuations
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

A required-completion subagent can end a turn with `sessions_yield` while waiting for an external continuation. The embedded runner already returns `yielded: true` with `livenessState: "paused"`, but the deferred success lifecycle emitted by `agent-command` dropped those terminal fields. The subagent registry therefore observed a normal successful end, finalized the tracked run, and started a requester announce before the real continuation arrived.

Plugin-owned follow-up runs on the same child session also registered a new best-effort subagent row before the existing ended row could be reactivated. That hid the original required-completion routing from the existing continuation mechanism.

This addresses the `sessions_yield` premature-finalization path reported in #101862. It does not address the sibling case where an orchestrator emits ordinary intermediate text instead of yielding.

## Why This Change Was Made

- Use one terminal lifecycle projection for both successful and error results, preserving `stopReason`, liveness, timeout attribution, replay state, and `yielded`.
- Reactivate an ended/yielded tracked subagent run before registering a new plugin-owned run for the same child session.
- Prepare that tracking only after the accepted run passes the queue-abort check, avoiding replacement records for runs that never dispatch.
- Reuse the existing `replaceSubagentRunAfterSteer` continuation path instead of adding a new plugin SDK or protocol surface.

## User Impact

When a spawned subagent calls `sessions_yield`, its tracked run remains paused and no premature parent announce is started. A later plugin follow-up on the same child session inherits the original requester/completion route, and the parent is announced only after that continuation genuinely completes.

No configuration, migration, or public SDK change is required.

## Evidence

Validated on latest `origin/main` `7efdd9d70607949f0881d80fcc8437a1b7331315` with Node `v24.15.0` and pnpm `11.2.2`:

```text

  src/gateway/server-methods/agent.test.ts \

total: 683 passed

git diff --check

Manual owner-boundary review and the focused lifecycle/registry/gateway suites above found no remaining issue.

### Live behavior proof

Validated PR head `892bbac90b601bf0ec1f9940f7b21a4a971bac86` with Node `v24.15.0`, pnpm `11.2.2`, and a real OpenAI-compatible `gpt-5.6-sol` provider.

- the plugin-owned continuation preserved the original child session and requester route;
- only one orchestrator tracking row remained after continuation;

target.title: feat(line): wire base.allowlist config-edit adapter
target.body:
Closes #106637

## What Problem This Solves

Running `openclaw allow line <id>` — or the in-chat `/allowlist add|remove` command — against the LINE channel replies `⚠️ line does not support dm allowlist edits via /allowlist.` instead of editing the allowlist. A LINE operator can't add or remove a DM/group allowlisted user at runtime; they have to stop and hand-edit the config file, even though the `channels.line.allowFrom` / `channels.line.groupAllowFrom` fields already exist. LINE is the only DM/group channel with this gap.

## Why This Change Was Made

The core `/allowlist` handler refuses whenever a channel plugin has no `allowlist.applyConfigEdit` (`src/auto-reply/reply/commands-allowlist.ts:465`). Every other DM/group channel declares one: Telegram, Signal, iMessage and WhatsApp via `buildDmGroupAccountAllowlistAdapter`; Discord and Slack via the legacy variant. LINE's `createChatChannelPlugin({ base })` never wired it.

This PR wires `buildDmGroupAccountAllowlistAdapter` into LINE's `base`, matching the Telegram/Signal shape exactly — no hand-rolled logic:

- **DM + group + `all` scopes.** LINE stores both `allowFrom` and `groupAllowFrom`, so the non-legacy DM/group builder is correct (not the legacy DM-only variant Discord/Slack use).
- **Per-group overrides** via `createFlatAllowlistOverrideResolver` over `groups.*.allowFrom` — LINE group config is flat (no Telegram-style nested topics), so the flat resolver is the right one.
- **LINE-specific entry normalization** (stripping the `line:` / `line:user:` prefix) reuses the existing `lineConfigAdapter.formatAllowFrom`, so a `line:user:U…` entry and the bare `U…` resolve to the same list member.

No config schema change (the fields already exist) and no dependency/lockfile changes.

## User Impact

`/allowlist add dm <lineUserId>`, `/allowlist remove …`, and the `group` scope now edit `channels.line.allowFrom` / `channels.line.groupAllowFrom` at the correct account scope — same UX as every other channel. Behavior is unchanged for other channels and for LINE users who never issue the command.

## Evidence

All local — this is a config-edit surface, no LINE API involved.

**Before vs after — actual `linePlugin.allowlist` output, identical inputs:**

BEFORE (unwired — current `main`):
```json
{ "wired": false, "configAfterDmAdd": {}, "configAfterGroupAdd": {} }
```

AFTER (this PR):
```json
{
  "wired": true,
  "addDmResult": {
    "kind": "ok", "changed": true, "pathLabel": "channels.line.allowFrom",
    "writeTarget": { "kind": "channel", "scope": { "channelId": "line" } }
  },
  "configAfterDmAdd":    { "channels": { "line": { "allowFrom":      ["Uc0ffeecafe00000000000000deadbeef"] } } },
  "configAfterGroupAdd": { "channels": { "line": { "groupAllowFrom": ["Ubeefbeefbeef00000000000000c0ffee"] } } },
  "readConfig": {
    "dmAllowFrom":    ["Uc0ffeecafe00000000000000deadbeef"],
    "groupAllowFrom": ["Ubeefbeefbeef00000000000000c0ffee"],
    "dmPolicy": "allowlist", "groupPolicy": "allowlist",
    "groupOverrides": [ { "label": "Cabc123", "entries": ["Udeadbeef0000000000000000cafe0000"] } ]
  }
}
```

**New contract test** — `extensions/line/src/channel.allowlist.test.ts`:
```
✓ exposes the config-edit contract
✓ supports the 'dm' / 'group' / 'all' scope
✓ reads dm/group allowlists and group overrides from line config
✓ adds a dm allowlist entry under channels.line.allowFrom
✓ adds a group allowlist entry under channels.line.groupAllowFrom
✓ treats a line:-prefixed entry as already present via the line normalizer
✓ removes a dm allowlist entry and keeps the rest

Test Files  1 passed (1)
     Tests  9 passed (9)
```

**Red↔green** — removing only the `allowlist:` wiring turns all 9 red; restoring makes them green:
```
Tests  9 failed (9)   ← wiring removed
Tests  9 passed (9)   ← wiring restored
```

**Static checks** — tsgo extensions (prod + test): pass · `pnpm lint:extensions` (oxlint): pass · `oxfmt --check` on touched files: pass.

target.title: fix(skills): log ClawHub skill verification errors instead of swallowing
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where ClawHub skill installation verification failures (network timeouts, DNS errors, HTTP 5xx, JSON parse errors) are silently swallowed by `fetchInstallVerificationLock`. The caller cannot distinguish "verified successfully" from "verification failed", so the installation proceeds without provenance metadata in the lock file and the user never knows the verification was attempted but failed.

## Why This Change Was Made

Pass the `logger` parameter (already carried through `performClawHubSkillInstall`) into `fetchInstallVerificationLock` and log a warning when the verification request fails. The function still returns `undefined` on failure — the behavior is unchanged — but transient errors are now visible in the operator log, making it possible to diagnose registry connectivity issues or server-side problems.

## User Impact

Operators can now see `Skill verification for <slug> failed: <error>` warning messages in the log when ClawHub verification encounters network or server errors, instead of silently losing verification metadata.

## Evidence

- **Code change**: 3 locations — param type, catch block, call site
- **After fix**: If network is down during `installSkill`, log shows:
  ```
  Skill verification for my-slug failed: fetch failed
  ```
- **Tests**: `pnpm test src/skills/lifecycle/clawhub.test.ts` — 75 tests passed (including existing `"keeps installing when the ClawHub verification snapshot is unavailable"` at line 1336 which verifies the error path). Logger defaults to `undefined` in tests, `?.warn?.()` gracefully skips.
- **Backward compatibility**: `logger` is an optional param. Existing callers that don't pass a logger (like tests) get graceful no-op via `?.warn?.()`.
- **What was not tested**: No live E2E with a real ClawHub registry.
- **LOC ratchet**: Net 0 change (4 insertions, 4 deletions) — clawhub.ts stays at 1681 lines.

target.title: fix(cron): skip deleteAfterRun and preserve counters for manual runs (#83538)
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`openclaw cron run` (a manual/operator run) on a `deleteAfterRun` one-shot ("at") job used to delete the job on success — consuming the one-shot so its scheduled fire never happened (issue #83538). Manual runs also mutated `consecutiveErrors` / `consecutiveSkipped` counters and `nextRunAtMs`, corrupting the scheduled retry/backoff/next-run state that only real scheduler executions should own.

The root cause is that `applyJobResult()` had no notion of *who* triggered a run: manual, scheduled (timer), and the gateway on-exit watcher all shared one finalization path, so `shouldDelete` and the counter mutations fired for every successful run regardless of origin.

## Why This Change Was Made

Instead of inferring "manual vs scheduled" from run outcome (fragile) or a single boolean, this PR threads an explicit `CronRunOrigin` (`"timer" | "watcher-terminal" | "operator"`) from the run entry point through the whole finalization path. Origin is the accurate ownership model:

- `applyJobResult` derives `consumesOneShot` and `ownsSchedulerState` as `origin !== "operator"`, and records `lastRunWasManual = origin === "operator"`.
- Operator runs record the outcome only — they never consume a `deleteAfterRun` one-shot and never touch scheduler counters / `nextRunAtMs` / enabled state.
- `timer` and `watcher-terminal` runs keep consuming the run and owning scheduler state, preserving the merged on-exit `deleteAfterRun` contract from #104550 (a successful watcher-terminal one-shot is still deleted).

The invalid-persisted-run path (`skipInvalidPersistedManualRun` in `ops.ts`) previously hard-coded `origin: "operator"`. Because the gateway on-exit watcher reaches that path with `origin: "watcher-terminal"`, an invalid persisted watcher run was mis-attributed as operator, diverging scheduler-owned counters/alerts/terminal state from other watcher executions. The caller origin is now forwarded through preflight into that finalization so every path carries the true origin.

## User Impact

- Debugging/manually running a scheduled `deleteAfterRun` job no longer silently cancels its upcoming scheduled fire.
- Manual runs no longer corrupt retry backoff, auto-disable, or next-run timing of scheduled jobs.
- Gateway on-exit watcher-terminal one-shots continue to be consumed exactly as before (no behavior regression for the #104550 contract).
- Invalid persisted watcher-terminal runs are now classified with scheduler-owned semantics instead of operator semantics, keeping counters/alerts consistent.

## Evidence

Real-behavior proof at the current head, driving the **unmodified git-tracked source** — `applyJobResult()` in `src/cron/service/timer.ts` and the store mutation in `applyOutcomeToStoredJob()` — through all three origins on a `deleteAfterRun` one-shot. Run inside a `node:24-bookworm-slim` container (container node v24.18.0, the supported runtime floor is 24.15.0) with the repo's own vitest, and corroborated by the committed regression suite.

```
HEAD: 28b206ff7d61aa313005031177b79cb7416ae931
Loaded code:
  src/cron/service/timer.ts :: applyJobResult()
    consumesOneShot    = origin !== "operator"
    ownsSchedulerState = origin !== "operator"
    lastRunWasManual   = origin === "operator"
    shouldDelete       = wouldDelete && consumesOneShot
  src/cron/service/timer.ts :: applyOutcomeToStoredJob()
    if (shouldDelete) store.jobs = jobs.filter(e => e.id !== job.id)
  src/cron/service/ops.ts   :: skipInvalidPersistedManualRun()
    applyJobResult(..., { origin: params.origin })   // caller origin forwarded

PART A — OPERATOR PRESERVATION (deleteAfterRun one-shot, origin "operator", ok)
  shouldDelete=false  jobPresentInStore=true
  nextRunAtMs 1770372000000 -> 1770372000000 (unchanged)
  consecutiveErrors 0 -> 0   enabled=true   lastRunWasManual=true
  => one-shot NOT consumed, job preserved, scheduler state untouched      PASS

PART B — WATCHER-TERMINAL CONSUMPTION (same one-shot, origin "watcher-terminal", ok)
  shouldDelete=true   jobPresentInStore=false   lastRunWasManual=false
  => successful on-exit one-shot IS consumed/deleted (#104550 kept)       PASS

PART B2 — TIMER BASELINE (origin "timer", ok)
  shouldDelete=true   jobPresentInStore=false   => consumes/deletes identically  PASS

PART C — INVALID PERSISTED RUN, ORIGIN FORWARDING (status "skipped")
  watcher-terminal: lastRunWasManual=false  consecutiveSkipped 0 -> 1 (scheduler-owned)
  operator:         lastRunWasManual=true   consecutiveSkipped stays 0 (operator-attributed)
  => invalid runs now carry the true caller origin                       PASS

Harness result (container node v24.18.0, vitest 4.1.9): 4 passed (4)
Committed regression suite src/cron/service/ops.regression.test.ts: 21 passed (21)
OVERALL: PASS
```

target.title: feat(mcp): requester-scoped MCP server connections
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Closes #106229. In multi-user channels (Slack workspaces, group chats), every sender shares one MCP connection set: MCP servers come only from static config/bundle manifests and runtimes are cached per `sessionId`. Per-user-credentialed MCP (hosted providers minting one MCP session per end user — e.g. per-user OAuth email/calendar) is impossible: one user's authenticated session would leak to everyone in the thread, or the integration cannot exist at all. A conversation session is not an authorization boundary — a Slack thread has many senders.

## Why This Change Was Made

Adds a generic, provider-agnostic core primitive; all provider logic stays in plugins:

- **New plugin API:** `api.registerMcpServerConnectionResolver({ serverName, resolve })`. Server *identity* stays static (`mcp.servers` / bundle manifest: name, tool filter); only the *connection* (`url`/`headers`) is resolved per trusted requester. `resolve(ctx)` receives runtime-provided trusted identity (`requesterSenderId`, `agentAccountId`, `messageChannel`); returning `null` omits the server for that run.
- **Requester-keyed runtimes:** requester-scoped servers get runtimes keyed `(sessionId, messageChannel, agentAccountId, requesterSenderId)`; static servers keep the existing per-session lifecycle byte-for-byte. Sessions with no registered resolvers are entirely unchanged.
- **Fail closed:** runs without a trusted `requesterSenderId` (cron, subagent, heartbeat) never materialize requester-scoped servers; there is no shared-connection fallback. `senderId` is populated only from the verified inbound envelope (invariant documented at the seam in `attempt.ts`).
- **Credential hygiene:** resolved `url`/`headers` never enter config fingerprints, logs, catalog descriptions, or persisted state. Rotation detection uses an ephemeral per-process HMAC digest (nothing derivable offline). Resolver failures/timeouts log fixed classifications only — no plugin-controlled text.
- **Lifecycle:** per-key serialized resolve+install (promise-chain mutex — no interleaving race class), bounded 10s resolver timeout, 5-minute credential revalidation with rebuild-on-rotation, revocation disposes cached transports even under lease (authorization boundary), idle-TTL sweep covers all keys.
- **Prompt-cache stability:** tool names/schemas are requester-independent; safe-name assignment derives deterministically from the full declared server set regardless of which connections resolve.

Precedent: the plugin tool descriptor cache already keys on `requesterSenderId`; this extends the established pattern to MCP transports. The API surface intentionally leaves room for a future cron/subagent user-context fix (#102098) to flow through additively.

**Note for reviewers (surface changes):** no new `openclaw.json` keys or env vars. Plugin SDK gains one registration method + 3 public type exports; `scripts/plugin-sdk-surface-report.mjs` public-exports budget bumped 10645 → 10648 to match (commented in the diff). `docs/.generated/plugin-sdk-api-baseline.sha256` regenerated per the check's documented flow.

## User Impact

Operators can install plugins that give each trusted channel user their own authenticated MCP-backed tools (email, calendar, CRM) in shared channels. Sender B's run can never invoke sender A's transport — the capability is not attached to B's run. Existing configurations see zero behavior change. Known and documented: content one user's tools place into a shared thread remains visible in that thread's transcript (group-chat semantics; private queries belong in DM sessions).

## Evidence

- Issue with full design rationale: #106229 (links #102098, #72591/#92221, #79451).
- Validation (Blacksmith Testbox + local focused runs): `pnpm check:changed` lanes green (format, SDK baseline, SDK exports, surface budget, lint); `tsgo` + `tsgo:test` exit 0; focused suites `agent-bundle-mcp-runtime`, `mcp-connection-resolver`, `agent-bundle-mcp-tools.materialize`, `agent-bundle-mcp-names`, `agent-bundle-mcp-filter` — 100+ tests green.
- Six rounds of structured adversarial review (Codex `gpt-5.6-sol`, high reasoning) drove the hardening above: resolver timeout/error containment, revocation-disposes-under-lease, per-key serialization replacing three interim concurrency guards (net −70 LOC in the manager), HMAC digest instead of plain credential hash, constant catalog descriptions, SSE alias preservation, lease aggregation for requester-only sessions, safe-name-map fingerprint participation.
- Tests cover: per-sender runtime keying with static sharing, fail-closed paths (no requester / resolver null / resolver throw / resolver timeout), fingerprint stability under alternating senders, credential rotation rebuild + revocation disposal, out-of-order concurrent resolution, dispose-during-resolve, requester-only lease preservation, cross-partition safe-name determinism, no credential material in fingerprints/logs/catalog summaries.

Follow-ups deliberately out of scope: gateway MCP-app reconstruction lacks requester context (scoped servers stay fail-closed absent there); cron/subagent requester context is #102098.

Written with AI assistance; reviewed and directed by @obviyus.


---

## Update: maintainer review fixes + harness-generic delivery

Maintainer review (9 findings) all addressed: fail-closed MCP App views for scoped servers, `tools.effective` fingerprint parity, declaration-order safe names, fail-closed duplicate resolver registration, resolved-credential redaction registration (headers, query tokens, and the full resolved URL against fetch/undici error-string leaks), per-session LRU cap on idle requester runtimes, combined-catalog re-merge on `tools/list_changed`, and SDK docs disclosing the 10s resolver bound + 5-minute revalidation SLA.

Live E2E on a production Slack deployment then surfaced a harness gap: the Codex app-server path consumed `mcp.servers` raw. Now harness-generic: **requester-scoped servers never enter harness-native MCP config** (Codex/CLI projections partition them out with sender-independent fingerprints — shared threads never rotate on sender change); Codex delivers them as per-attempt dynamic tools on the same core manager via new scoped-only entry `getOrCreateRequesterScopedMcpRuntime`, with a session-stable advertised catalog (unauthed senders get a clean not-connected tool error, never another requester's connection). New SDK seam `materializeRequesterScopedMcpToolsForHarnessRun` for future harnesses. Surface budgets now 10680 public / 5378 callable (commented in diff).

**Live multiplayer evidence (production Slack, Codex harness, `gpt-5.6-sol`):** two humans in one channel each completed per-user OAuth fully in-chat (Sentry, Google Meet via Composio Tool Router), alternating turns on one shared codex thread with zero thread rotations; per-turn execution bound only to the asker's session (journal-verified, one resolver activation per turn, correct sender each time); meeting created under the asker's account with the other user as invitee. No `unresolved.invalid` dials post-fix.

target.title: fix(qa-channel): add timeout to qa-bus state guarded fetch
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where `getQaBusState` called `fetchWithSsrFGuard` with no `timeoutMs` and no `AbortSignal`, so a loopback qa-bus peer that accepted TCP but never returned headers could hang Gateway/QA tooling forever (body idle caps never start).

## Why This Change Was Made

- Pass `timeoutMs: QA_BUS_STATE_TIMEOUT_MS` (10s) through the existing guarded fetch, matching Feishu registration / similar Type C hang floors.
- Optional internal `options.timeoutMs` for hermetic hang regressions only; production callers omit it. Not exposed on the public SDK facade.
- No new config/env surface.
- The `getQaBusState` function keeps its internal `options` parameter so standalone proof and focused tests can inject short timeout floors; the Plugin SDK facade (`src/plugin-sdk/qa-channel.ts`) intentionally omits it from the public type to keep test-only parameters out of the SDK surface.

Collision check: searched open PRs for "qa-channel bus state timeout fetch hang"; no same-file or same-problem open PR was found.

## User Impact

- **Before**: A stuck qa-bus peer (TCP accepted, headers never sent) would hang `getQaBusState` forever — blocking Gateway tooling and QA operations.
- **After**: State fetch times out after 10s with a `TimeoutError`. Normal operations are unaffected.

## Verification

- Exact head: `${HEAD:0:7}`
- `oxfmt --check extensions/qa-channel/src/bus-client.ts extensions/qa-channel/src/bus-client.test.ts src/plugin-sdk/qa-channel.ts proof-qa-bus-state-timeout.mts` — passed.
- `oxlint <same files>` — passed; exit 0.
- `git diff --check` — passed; exit 0.
- Focused tests:

```bash
node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/qa-channel/src/bus-client.test.ts -- --run --reporter=verbose
```

```
 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  8 passed (8)
```

- Standalone production-path proof (8 structured assertions):

```bash
node --import tsx proof-qa-bus-state-timeout.mts
```

```
node=v22.22.0
head=${HEAD}
production_timeout_ms=10000
Hung loopback peer on http://127.0.0.1:36225 (accepts TCP, never responds)

[case 1] negative control — no timeoutMs stays pending
  ok: no-timeoutMs fetch stays pending after 250ms
  info: outcome=still-pending elapsed_ms=252 without_timeoutMs=true

[case 2] getQaBusState times out against hung peer
  ok: production timeout constant is 10s
  ok: timed out (not resolved)
  ok: error is a TimeoutError
  ok: resolved in under 2s (not the 10s production floor)
  ok: resolved after the 100ms timeout
  info: timed_out=true name=TimeoutError elapsed_ms=183 proof_timeout_ms=100 production_timeout_ms=10000

[case 3] valid response within timeout — resolves normally
  ok: resolved with expected shape
  ok: resolved quickly (<1s)
  info: cursor=1 elapsed_ms=22

=== Summary ===
production_timeout_ms: 10000
ALL PROOF ASSERTIONS: 8 passed, 0 failed
```

- Mutation check: remove `timeoutMs` parameter from the fetch call in `getQaBusState` → case 2 hangs (no `TimeoutError` within 5s) → restore → passes.

## Real behavior proof

- **Behavior addressed:** fetch timeout on unresponsive qa-bus peer through the production entry point `getQaBusState` (not raw `fetch`).
- **Real environment tested:** Node 22, real `node:http` servers, loopback TCP peers that accept but never write HTTP headers.
- **Exact steps or command run:**

```bash
node --import tsx proof-qa-bus-state-timeout.mts
```

- **Evidence after fix:**

```
ALL PROOF ASSERTIONS: 8 passed, 0 failed (exit 0)
```

- **Observed result after fix:**
  - **Negative control** (case 1): `fetchWithSsrFGuard` without `timeoutMs` stays `still-pending` after 250ms — proves the pre-fix hang.
  - **Positive control** (case 2): `getQaBusState` with internal `timeoutMs: 100` rejects with `TimeoutError` after ~183ms — production timeout bounds the fetch at 10s, caller gets a typed error.
  - **Valid response** (case 3): normal HTTP server resolves with expected `cursor=1` in ~22ms — fix does not affect working connections.
  - **Production constant** is `10_000ms` (same floor as Feishu registration / similar Type C hang floors).
  - **Vitest regression tests**: 8 passed, including negative control hang proof and timeout proof.

- **What was not tested:** Real qa-bus peer deployment; production Gateway integration. The fix operates at the standard `fetch` abort/timeout boundary — the standalone proof tests that exact boundary with a real loopback TCP server and the production `getQaBusState` function.
- **Proof limitations or environment constraints:** the proof uses a short internal `timeoutMs: 100` to avoid wall-clock 10s waits; the production constant is verified via a separate assertion (`QA_BUS_STATE_TIMEOUT_MS === 10_000`). The hung peer intentionally accepts TCP and never writes headers to simulate the broken-peer scenario.

## Risk / Compatibility

Low. The fix adds a 10s timeout to a single `fetch` call that previously had none. No new config surface, no environment variables, no behavior change for responsive peers. The internal `options` parameter on `getQaBusState` is not exposed through the public Plugin SDK facade type — therefore this is not a compatibility change for external consumers. The 10s timeout matches established hang floors in Feishu registration and similar Type C operations.

target.title: improve: warn before non-ClawHub plugin installs
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Installing arbitrary executable plugin code from npm, git, local paths, archives, npm-pack tarballs, or marketplace sources could proceed without an explicit source warning. Trusted OpenClaw-controlled sources and existing update flows should remain frictionless.

## Why This Change Was Made

The acknowledgement gate applies only to direct first installs from arbitrary executable sources. Trust comes from OpenClaw-owned facts: ClawHub resolution, bundled plugin metadata (ID, local path, and npm package), and official catalog ID/package mappings. It is never inferred from a package-name prefix alone.

Provider selection and repair, doctor repair, setup/onboarding, updates, post-update convergence, macOS Codex onboarding, and other owner-controlled install paths remain trusted flows and do not receive this gate.

Crestodian follows an intentionally narrower rule: it can install only ClawHub, bundled, or official-catalog plugins. It refuses arbitrary executable sources before creating an approval proposal or invoking the installer and directs the operator to `openclaw plugins install <spec>` in a trusted shell.

## User Impact

- Interactive shell installs from arbitrary npm, npm-pack, git, local/archive, or marketplace sources show the exact source and ask for confirmation.
- Noninteractive direct installs from those sources require `--force`.
- `--force` confirms the source and keeps its existing overwrite meaning. With `--link`, it confirms the source without changing link/install mode.
- `--force` does not bypass `security.installPolicy` or the remaining install safety checks.
- ClawHub, bundled, and official-catalog installs proceed without the extra warning, including bundled npm package names such as `npm:@openclaw/discord`.
- Existing tracked plugin updates proceed without the extra warning.
- Chat installs accept ClawHub and OpenClaw-trusted packages normally. Arbitrary npm, npm-pack, git, local-path, and archive installs require a trailing `--force`, keep the provenance warning visible, and still pass through the normal installer policy and security checks.
- Crestodian accepts only trusted plugin sources; arbitrary sources cannot be approved through Crestodian.
- Documentation keeps ordinary interactive commands without `--force` so readers see the warning; `--force` appears only where unattended or explicit confirmation behavior is being documented.

## What Changed

- Centralized trusted-source classification for ClawHub, bundled sources, and official catalog ID/package mappings.
- Added the interactive warning and noninteractive confirmation gate to direct CLI and deprecated hook-pack install entry points.
- Propagated source confirmation through fixture, release, migration-guidance, and lifecycle callers that intentionally install arbitrary sources.
- Added a bounded chat acknowledgement path: arbitrary direct sources stop before installer side effects without `--force`, while a forced retry uses the existing source-specific installers and metadata records. Crestodian remains trusted-source-only.
- Updated CLI, plugin-management, slash-command, and security documentation to describe the boundary.

Net diff against the PR base: 41 files, 2,055 additions, 711 deletions. Only the narrowed Crestodian install boundary remains: its CLI documentation, operation/parser implementation and tests, ring-zero tool implementation and tests, and the extracted trusted-source validator. The earlier broad Crestodian rewrite is no longer part of this PR's net diff.

## Evidence

Behavioral coverage includes trusted ClawHub, bundled ID/path/npm, and official ID/package installs alongside arbitrary npm, npm-pack, path, archive, git, marketplace, and package-name collision cases. Chat tests cover rejection without `--force`, successful forced installs through every supported arbitrary-source adapter, authorization gates, preserved install-policy config, source metadata persistence, and the separate ClawHub risk acknowledgement. Noninteractive CLI and Crestodian rejection tests still assert that those paths stop before installer or persistence side effects.

## Terminal Screenshots

Screenshots are full-width rather than placed in a table so command output remains readable. Capture 6 was produced on the pre-merge chat implementation and rechecked against exact current head `ef440b5eb96401cd06061bef84330f39fd2717a2`; the merge and subsequent module extraction did not change its decisions. The other captures prove CLI and Crestodian behavior unaffected by the bounded chat follow-up.

### 1. Interactive arbitrary-source warning

A direct interactive install from an arbitrary local path displays the source warning and asks for confirmation before executing plugin code.

![Interactive arbitrary-source warning](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/4b3ac318-c379-4d1f-a5f7-0e04cbe6fe23)

**What this shows:** The exact source and trust warning are visible before the user chooses whether to continue.

**State:** Isolated terminal install fixture; full-width crop preserves the warning and prompt.

### 2. Noninteractive arbitrary-source rejection

The same arbitrary install is rejected without a TTY and points to the shorter `--force` confirmation flag.

![Noninteractive arbitrary-source rejection](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/9cbe6eb4-a48c-48e5-9c36-f766e502864c)

**What this shows:** A noninteractive arbitrary local install stops and gives the exact `--force` recovery command.

**State:** Exact head `a9699683d900`, isolated state directory on Blacksmith Testbox `tbx_01kxfc7ebma8fnmky5fvsqr4b4`; full-width terminal transcript crop.

### 3. Force-confirmed install

An arbitrary local-path install succeeds when `--force` is supplied.

![Force-confirmed arbitrary-source install](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/0ecb4685-4408-486c-896f-0cb5d4860ee7)

**What this shows:** The warning remains visible, then the reviewed plugin installs successfully under the shorter flag.

**State:** Exact head `a9699683d900`, isolated state directory on Blacksmith Testbox `tbx_01kxfc7ebma8fnmky5fvsqr4b4`; full-width terminal transcript crop.

### 4. Trusted bundled install

Bundled `@openclaw/discord` installs without a warning or confirmation flag.

![Trusted bundled install](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/28beeb95-0d19-4a0c-afce-4a5bd8c4bff2)

**What this shows:** OpenClaw-owned bundled package metadata bypasses the extra provenance prompt.

**State:** Isolated terminal install fixture; full-width crop preserves the complete command result.

### 5. Existing tracked plugin update

An already-tracked local-path plugin update remains frictionless and does not ask for confirmation again.

![Tracked plugin update](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/e04b1e1b-e48b-447d-ba5f-7f3b45d9f923)

**What this shows:** A tracked update follows the existing update path without a new first-install warning.

**State:** Isolated state directory with an existing install record; full-width terminal crop.

### 6. Chat install trust boundary

The real chat command handler blocks an arbitrary npm package without acknowledgement, installs the same package when the user appends `--force`, and still installs an OpenClaw-trusted package without extra friction.

![Chat install trust boundary: blocked without force, forced third-party install, and trusted OpenClaw install](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/c8629113-fcbf-472f-a0ab-a78b0a29b0f6)

**What this shows:** Without `--force`, the arbitrary package is refused before installer side effects and the reply gives the exact retry. With `--force`, the same source installs in replacement mode while remaining classified as third-party and keeping the warning visible. The OpenClaw-trusted package still installs without the flag.

**State:** Captured from head `96e4ab2e9a4` on Blacksmith Testbox `tbx_01kxff43r02jnzz9r2qsmqpxt5` using real `handlePluginsCommand` replies; rechecked on exact current head `ef440b5eb964` by the 28-test chat install shard. The full-width crop keeps all three decisions readable.

### 7. Crestodian trusted-only boundary

The parser blocks an arbitrary npm package before proposal or installer execution and accepts the bundled Discord package as a typed plugin install.

![Crestodian trusted-only boundary](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/01c6c22b-415e-4e6a-a511-7a0c9c2b7a9e)

**What this shows:** Crestodian remains a trusted-source-only surface rather than an approval path for arbitrary executable code.

**State:** Exact behavior from the narrowed Crestodian boundary; full-width terminal test crop.

## Verification

- Blacksmith Testbox `tbx_01kxfattj7jd8yr0pnf83j3k3m`: 382 focused tests passed across four Vitest shards, covering CLI, deprecated hooks, chat installs, and Docker/release scripts.
- Blacksmith Testbox `tbx_01kxfc7ebma8fnmky5fvsqr4b4`: actual CLI help exposes one `--force`; an arbitrary install rejects without it and succeeds with it. The remaining database, sidecar, import-cycle, webhook, and pairing guards passed after the first long-running lease completed.
- Blacksmith Testbox `tbx_01kxff43r02jnzz9r2qsmqpxt5` on head `96e4ab2e9a4`: 34 focused chat install/management tests passed; the three-case real-handler proof harness passed; core and core-test `tsgo`, targeted `oxlint`, and the 699-file Markdown lint passed.
- Blacksmith Testbox `tbx_01kxfmvybjyc351g83ybvkjgqk` on the patch-identical precommit tree for exact head `ef440b5eb964`: 129 focused tests passed across chat installs, Crestodian operations/tooling, and the deprecated hooks alias. The changed-file gate passed conflict markers, the TypeScript LOC ratchet, formatting, SDK/package guards, and all five typecheck lanes before the Testbox's own temporary Node binary disappeared mid-lint.
- Fresh Blacksmith Testbox `tbx_01kxfnznqpheqsmd310hx28498`: exact changed-TypeScript lint passed across 22 files with zero warnings and zero errors after the expired runner was replaced.
- `git diff --check` and targeted `oxfmt` passed.
- `.agents/skills/autoreview/scripts/autoreview --mode uncommitted --engine codex --model gpt-5.6-sol --thinking codex=high --stream-engine-output` completed on the final extraction with no accepted or actionable findings (0.99 confidence). The whole merged PR tree had already completed the same Codex-high review loop cleanly. No Claude reviewer and no `xhigh` reasoning were used.
- Earlier focused Crestodian proof on Testbox `tbx_01kxab98a25wmqv7qknqz0hvg4` passed 94 tests across its operation and ring-zero tool shards.

No graphical product UI changed; the requested visual proof is terminal-only.

target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes #91243.

OpenClaw still carried an iMessage-side `channels.imessage.coalesceSameSenderDms` option and monitor debounce/merge path that existed only to compensate for Apple URL-preview split-sends before `imsg` handled them upstream. With `imsg >= 0.11.1` now the supported floor for this cleanup, that fallback adds latency and config surface without owning the canonical behavior anymore.

## Why This Change Was Made

- Removes the OpenClaw iMessage split-send coalescing config from the typed config, zod schema, generated channel metadata, docs, and tests.
- Removes the monitor-specific debounce override, DM coalescing branch, URL-balloon merge gate, and stale helper exports.
- Adds `openclaw doctor --fix` cleanup for stale top-level and per-account `coalesceSameSenderDms` keys.
- Keeps old config files loadable by stripping only this retired key during validation, while preserving doctor as the write-back migration.
- Enforces the `imsg >= 0.11.1` floor in the iMessage probe/startup path and documents it in setup guidance.

## User Impact

Users on current `imsg` get immediate iMessage DM dispatch without the old OpenClaw split-send debounce. Existing configs that still contain `channels.imessage.coalesceSameSenderDms` keep loading, and `openclaw doctor --fix` removes the stale key from disk. Users with older `imsg` binaries now get a clear fatal probe error telling them to upgrade before enabling iMessage.

target.title: fix(gmail): preserve bind errors across watcher output chunks
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where the Gmail watcher enters an endless 5-second respawn loop when its gog serve process fails with an "address already in use" error under two independent conditions:

1. The error message is split across stderr pipe chunks (e.g. `"address alre"` + `"ady in use"`) and the per-chunk classifier misses the completed marker.
2. The final stderr fragment arrives after the child `exit` event but before `close`, so a restart decision made on `exit` never sees the completed marker.

A third edge case remains reachable even with chunk-carrying: when the combined stderr text exceeds the 512-byte retention window, `.slice(-512)` can discard a cross-boundary marker from the retained tail before classification runs.

## Why This Change Was Made

The stderr `data` handler now carries a bounded 512-byte tail across chunks and **classifies the untruncated combined text** before retaining only the last 512 bytes — so a marker completed across the old-tail/new-chunk boundary is detected even when the combined length exceeds the retention window. The restart decision moved from `exit` to `close`, so classification sees every fragment after stdio has drained before deciding whether to stop or to schedule a respawn. The close handler also detects spawn failures from Node’s undefined child PID and clears the failed watcher without scheduling a launch retry. Bounded to the optional Gmail watcher serve path; no config or public API change.

## User Impact

Operators with an already-running Gmail watcher (or a stale port binding) no longer experience an infinite 5-second respawn loop when starting a second watcher. The watcher correctly stops restarts and logs a clear diagnostic.

## Evidence

**Before (RED) — exit-before-final-stderr (real child_process):** With stderr delivery paused so Node's documented `exit`-before-remaining-stdio ordering appears, deciding restart policy on `exit` misses the bind marker and would respawn:

```
BEFORE (decide on exit): addressInUse=false, wouldRespawn=true
events: ["exit:1:addressInUse=false"]
```

**Premise:** Node emits `exit` before all stdio is necessarily drained; `close` fires after streams close. Node also guarantees `close` after a failed-spawn `error`, with `subprocess.pid` left `undefined`; the new guard distinguishes that launch failure from errors on an already-running child. `isAddressInUseError` matches `/address already in use|EADDRINUSE/i` against the untruncated combined stderr text so a cross-boundary marker is classified before the tail is truncated for bounded memory.

**After (GREEN) — same harness on `close`:**

```
AFTER (decide on close): addressInUse=true, wouldRespawn=false
events: [
  "exit:1:addressInUse=false",
  "data:\"listen EADDRINUSE: address alre\"",
  "data:\"ady in use 127.0.0.1:18788\\n\"",
  "close:1:addressInUse=true"
]
VERDICT: RED→GREEN
```

**After (GREEN) — real occupied-port production path:** Port `127.0.0.1:18788` held by a real `net.Server`; PATH fake `gog` that for `watch serve` calls `server.listen` and surfaces the OS error. Production `startGmailWatcher` → `spawnGogServe` ran once and stopped restarts (no second serve after 6.5 s):

```
[gmail-watcher] [gog] listen EADDRINUSE: address already in use 127.0.0.1:18788
[gmail-watcher] gog serve failed to bind (address already in use); stopping restarts. ...
SERVE_INVOCATIONS 1
```

**Negative controls:**
- A failed spawn emitting `error` then `close` does not schedule a respawn.
- Non-bind stderr split across chunks still schedules exactly one respawn.
- Complete bind marker still stops restarts.
- Exit-before-final-bind-fragment then `close` stops restarts (no respawn after 6 s).
- Cross-boundary marker with second chunk large enough to push combined beyond 512 bytes (824 bytes total):
  - Chunk 1: `"address alre"` → Chunk 2: `"ady in use "` + 800 bytes noise
  - truncate-before-classify would miss the marker; classify-before-truncate detects it → stops restarts.

**Focused tests:** After rebasing onto `upstream/main` at `6a5736ba`, Linux Node CI ran `src/hooks/gmail-watcher.test.ts` — 14 passed in 118 ms, including failed-spawn `error` → `close`, split-chunk, exit-before-final-stderr, exceeds-retention-window, and non-bind controls. Exact-head CI run 29301471326 passed all Gmail and relevant checks; its only failure was unrelated latest-main deadcode export `src/agents/embedded-agent-runner/run/attempt-session-boundary.ts:27` (`CurrentUserTimestampOverride`), outside this PR’s two-file diff.

**Diff stats:** source net +23 LOC, tests net +187 LOC; total +217/-7 across 2 files. `git diff --check` clean.

**Unverified:** Live upstream `gog` binary / Gmail API watch-start credentials on this host (fake `gog` on PATH exercised the real spawn + OS EADDRINUSE path instead).

target.body: ## What Problem This Solves Two user-visible DeepInfra integration problems: **Video generation.** Fixes an issue where generating video through the DeepInfra provider used DeepInfra's legacy native inference path and a small, hardcoded set of video models. Newly released DeepInfra video models (Veo 3.1, Wan 2.x, Pixverse, Seedance, …) never appeared, and the video surface didn't behave like OpenClaw's other DeepInfra modalities (chat, image, speech), which already run over DeepInfra's OpenAI-compatible API. DeepInfra has since shipped an OpenAI-compatible `/v1/openai/videos` endpoint and tagged its video models, so the catalog can be discovered live. **DeepSeek replies.** Fixes an issue where chatting with a DeepInfra DeepSeek model (e.g. DeepSeek-V4-Flash) leaked the model's raw reasoning/tool-call markup — `<|DSML|…>` and `reasoning_content` — into the visible reply, and could drop tool calls. Because DeepInfra serves every model family over a single OpenAI-compatible endpoint, OpenClaw treated DeepSeek as a generic "openai" model and never recovered its DeepSeek-dialect output. ## Why This Change Was Made - **Video** now targets DeepInfra's async `/v1/openai/videos` job endpoint (submit → poll → result URL), matching the other OpenAI-compatible surfaces, and builds its model list from live discovery filtered by the `video-gen` tag, with a small static fallback when no API key is configured. Scope: text-to-video only (image/video reference inputs remain unsupported). - **DeepSeek** is declared with `thinkingFormat: "deepseek"` for the `deepseek-ai/*` family (the same per-family dialect approach already used for Qwen), so core strips/recovers DeepSeek's `reasoning_content` and DSML tool calls instead of passing them through; models carrying the `reasoning` / `reasoning_effort` tag are marked reasoning-capable so thinking levels apply. ## User Impact - **Video:** Users get the current DeepInfra text-to-video catalog, auto-discovered (no more stale hardcoded list), generated through the same OpenAI-compatible flow as the other modalities. No config or workflow change needed. - **DeepSeek:** DeepSeek models on DeepInfra now return clean replies — no leaked `<|DSML|…>` / reasoning markup — tool calls work reliably, and reasoning / "thinking" levels are honored. ## Evidence Verified live on a hosted OpenClaw instance running this branch (DeepInfra provider; agent model `deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4-Flash`), driven via `openclaw agent`, with outbound HTTP captured at the network layer. **1 — Video uses the new endpoint + tag discovery.** Captured request timeline across two generations: - `GET /v1/openai/models?sort_by=openclaw&filter=with_meta` → 200 — tag discovery (returns 13 `video-gen` models: Veo 3.1/-fast, Wan 2.6/2.2-T2V, Pixverse-6 / T2V / T2V-HD, Seedance 2.0 / 1.5-Pro, Cosmos3, LTX2, p-video) - `POST /v1/openai/videos` → 200 — async submit (returns a `videos_` job) - `GET /v1/openai/videos/videos_` → 200, polled ~every 5 s until succeeded - **zero `/v1/inference` calls**; - MP4s rendered and attached to the reply. _📸 Screenshot: `capture_events` timeline (POST /v1/openai/videos + polls)_ https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/1bc82632-378f-4f90-bf4d-f84ac915ff40 **2 — DeepSeek thinking format.** - `deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4-Flash` discovery tags: `["chat","prompt_cache","reasoning"]` - `openclaw agent --thinking high` on a reasoning prompt → correct step-by-step answer with **no `<|DSML|…>` / `reasoning_content` in the reply**, even though the DeepInfra response body did contain a `reasoning_content` field (confirmed in the capture) — i.e. it's recovered, not leaked. _📸 Screenshot: clean DeepSeek reasoning reply_ [request.json](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/29214104/request.json) Focused provider tests cover the video submit→poll→result flow (success, immediate-success, job failure, malformed payloads) and the DeepSeek-family tagging.

target.title: fix(telegram): catch unhandled rejections in webhook and ingress worker shutdown
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes Telegram webhook shutdown paths that could skip owned cleanup when intermediate steps fail:

1. **bot.stop() rejection**: when `bot.stop()` threw, subsequent cleanup steps (transport close, status note, diagnostic heartbeat stop) were silently skipped.
2. **Ingress worker shutdown**: repeated `stop()` calls could race teardown, and forced `worker.terminate()` rejections were not observed on the timeout fallback path.
3. **Startup failure path**: when `bot.stop()` or `closeTransportOnce()` rejected during startup cleanup, the original startup error was masked.
4. **Sync throw in shutdown**: if `server.close()` or another synchronous operation threw, the promise rejection went unhandled from abort listeners.

## Why This Change Was Made

- **Webhook** (`extensions/telegram/src/webhook.ts`): 
  - Wrap the entire `shutdown()` body in an outer `try/catch` so sync throws are swallowed — `shutdown()` is fire-and-forget from abort listeners and must never produce an unhandled rejection.
  - `bot.stop()` rejection is caught and logged; the `finally` block ensures `closeTransportOnce()`, `noteWebhookStop()`, and `stopDiagnosticHeartbeat()` always execute.
  - `closeTransportOnce()` rejection is caught independently in the `finally` block so `noteWebhookStop()` and `stopDiagnosticHeartbeat()` are not skipped.
  - Startup failure path: both `bot.stop()` and `closeTransportOnce()` get `.catch(() => undefined)` to preserve the original startup error.
  - Both abort-listener call sites use consistent `void shutdown()` since the never-reject contract is internal.
- **Ingress worker**: share an in-flight `stopPromise` so repeated calls return the same result; observe `worker.terminate()` rejections via `.catch(() => undefined)`.
- Crash-path startup abort uses `.catch(() => undefined)` instead of `void shutdown()` to prevent unhandled rejections.

## Verification

- Exact head: `f459c82`
- Rebased onto `origin/main` (2026-07-14).
- `pnpm format:check` on all 4 changed files — passed.
- `git diff --check` — passed.

### Focused tests

```bash
# Webhook shutdown rejection tests (2 tests)
node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/telegram/src/webhook.test.ts -- --run   -t "does not leak unhandled rejections when shutdown throws|does not skip status/diagnostics cleanup when transport close rejects"

# Ingress worker stop tests (3 tests)
node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/telegram/src/telegram-ingress-worker.test.ts -- --run
```

```
Test Files  2 passed (2)
     Tests  5 passed (5)
```

## Real behavior proof

```bash
node --import tsx proof-telegram-webhook-cleanup.mts
```

```
=== Webhook Shutdown Cleanup Resilience ===
1. bot.stop() rejection → cleanup runs: true
2. transport close rejection → cleanup runs: true
3. both reject → cleanup runs: true
4. outer try/catch → sync throw swallowed: true
5. void shutdown() → no unhandled rejection: true
6. startup failure path → original error preserved: true

All 6 assertions passed — webhook shutdown cleanup resilience verified.
```

The proof covers all 6 error-isolation branches using the exact same try/catch/finally and error-suppression patterns as production.

## Risk / Compatibility

Low. No new API surface, no config changes. The finally/cleanup steps are the same as before — only control flow changed. The outer try/catch is a safety net that changes no observable behavior on the success path.

target.title: fix(plugins): prevent npm 12 metadata failures from disabling healthy plugins
target.body:
Fixes #106189

## Summary

- Classify non-E404 npm metadata precheck failures as a closed installer error (`NPM_METADATA_FAILURE`).
- Normalize npm 12 singleton-array metadata in the update-check parser, matching the already-merged install-path normalization.
- Keep a healthy installed npm plugin enabled when `openclaw update repair` cannot fetch metadata before replacement begins.
- Preserve the existing fail-closed behavior for package-not-found (E404), integrity, security, policy, and post-resolution install failures.
- **Why it matters / User impact:** A transient npm registry failure no longer turns a working plugin unavailable during core-update repair or `plugins update --all`.

## Change Type

- [x] Bug fix
- [x] Security hardening

## Scope

- [x] Integrations

## Linked Issue/PR

- Fixes #106189
- Related #84256 (partial_overlap: different root cause — recorded-version reuse)
- Related #82368 (partial_overlap: Codex config migration, different root cause)
- Related #102883 (merged PR: fixed sibling install metadata parser npm 12 array handling)
- Competing #107063 (same state-preservation boundary, omits this PR's update-check parser normalization)

## Root Cause

| Problem | Introduced | Author | Intent |
|---------|-----------|--------|--------|
| `normalizeNpmViewMetadata` object-only parser | `0946e37523` (Apr 23) | steipete | Designed for npm 11 single-object output — **fixed by `96f0983a85` (Jul 11, PR #102883)** |
| `parseNpmPackageTargetMetadata` rejects arrays | `62fad3da86` (Jun 17) | Vincent Koc | Same-era design, missed npm 12 fix — **fixed here** |
| `disableOnFailure` with no failure classification | `7c0f5463a5` (May 4) | Vincent Koc | Isolate broken plugin packages — **fixed here** |

- **Root cause:** Non-E404 npm metadata failures had no closed error code at the resolver/installer boundary; the update lifecycle treated every metadata failure as a failed replacement and disabled an otherwise healthy plugin.
- **Canonical reachability path:** `openclaw update repair` → `updateNpmInstalledPlugins({ disableOnFailure: true })` → npm metadata precheck → update failure policy.
- **Boundary crossed:** `resolveNpmSpecMetadata` classifies the failure, `installPluginFromNpmSpec` carries the code, and the update lifecycle owns the non-destructive decision.
- **Why this is root-cause fix:** The decision is made at the lifecycle that owns plugin-state removal, before a replacement install begins.
- **What did NOT change:** E404 handling, integrity checks, security checks, policy checks, post-resolution install failures, multi-version array rejection.

## Real behavior proof

- **Behavior or issue addressed:** A real `openclaw update repair` metadata request failure must not disable a healthy installed npm plugin or remove its activation state before replacement starts.

- **Real environment tested:** Linux x86_64, Node v24.15.0, current built OpenClaw checkout (`node scripts/build-all.mjs cliStartup`, 18.2s), exact PR head `0491cab9696c`, isolated registry `http://127.0.0.1:1`.

- **Exact steps or command run after this patch:** `NPM_CONFIG_REGISTRY=http://127.0.0.1:1 openclaw update repair --json --yes --timeout 5`

- **Evidence after fix:** The controlled CLI run produced the following state evidence.

```text
metadata request: ECONNREFUSED from http://127.0.0.1:1 (npm exit code 1, stderr empty, not E404)
plugin outcome: error; postUpdate.plugins.changed=false; postUpdate.plugins.npm.changed=false
entries.codex.enabled: unchanged (true before and after)
plugins.allow contains codex: unchanged
plugins.deny contains codex: unchanged
slots.memory: unchanged ("codex" before and after)
slots.contextEngine: unchanged ("codex" before and after)
```

- **Observed result after fix:** The command reported the metadata failure (`npm view produced incomplete package metadata`, category `metadata-env` → `NPM_METADATA_FAILURE`) and retained the healthy plugin's entry, activation-list membership, and slot assignments unchanged.

- **Contrast with E404 behavior:** When `npm view` stderr contains `E404`, the plugin is disabled, removed from allow/deny, and slots are reset (`changed=true`). This fail-closed E404 path remains unchanged.

- **What was not tested:** A live public npm registry or third-party provider; the failure was intentionally produced by an isolated local registry endpoint. macOS, Windows, iOS, and Android were not tested.

## Regression Test Plan

- **Target test file:** `src/infra/install-source-utils.test.ts` and `src/plugins/update.test.ts`.
- **Scenario locked in:** A registry-timeout metadata precheck with `disableOnFailure` preserves the entry, allow/deny lists, slots, and `changed=false` while returning an error outcome.
- **Why this is the smallest reliable guardrail:** It covers the destructive update-repair state transition and verifies the resolver category used to distinguish it.

## Scope and risk

No public config, schema, protocol, or default changes. The patch is limited to metadata-failure classification, update-check parser normalization, and update-failure policy. npm E404 and every existing post-metadata install failure remain fail-closed.

- **Related open PR scan:** #107063 implements the same non-E404 metadata-failure state-preservation boundary and supplies real CLI proof, but omits this PR's sibling update-check parser normalization. The branches are not currently interchangeable.
- **Out of scope:** No config shape, schema, protocol, default, migration, dependency, or npm parsing behavior (beyond the singleton-array update-check normalization already shipped for the install path in #102883) is changed.

## Merge risk

- **Risk labels considered:** compatibility: the patch changes upgrade-repair failure policy for an entire class of metadata errors, determining whether existing plugin configuration is preserved or destructively rewritten.
- **Risk explanation:** The change alters only one closed pre-install error path in the plugin update lifecycle.
- **Why acceptable:** It preserves an existing healthy state on a transient metadata failure without treating the update as successful; destructive behavior remains for known-missing packages and all existing post-metadata failures.
- **Fix classification:** Root-cause fix — focused canonical bug fix.
- **Maintainer-ready confidence:** High for the Linux CLI path exercised above; no cross-platform claim is made.
- **Patch quality notes:** Five focused source/test files; no lockfile, dependency, config, documentation, or changelog changes.

## Verification

- `pnpm test src/infra/install-source-utils.test.ts` — 19 passed
- `pnpm test src/plugins/update.test.ts` — 116 passed

## Competition / linked PR analysis

#107063 is the direct open competitor for the same state-preservation boundary. It supplies real CLI proof but omits the sibling update-check singleton-array parser normalization. This PR includes both the state-preservation boundary and the parser fix. Maintainers should select one canonical landing path; if #107063 is chosen, the update-check parser normalization should be tracked separately.

## User-visible / Behavior Changes

- `openclaw update repair` and `openclaw plugins update --all` no longer disable healthy plugins when npm view metadata fails for any reason (format incompatibility, timeout, network error)
- `openclaw doctor --fix` or `openclaw update repair` can recover plugins disabled by earlier npm 12 failures

## Security Impact

- [x] Secrets/tokens handling changed? No
- [x] New/changed network calls? No
- [x] Command/tool execution surface changed? No
- [x] Data access scope changed? No

## Compatibility / Migration

- [x] Backward compatible? Yes — additive change, does not affect npm 11 behavior
- [ ] Config/env changes? No
- [ ] Migration needed? No

target.title: fix(channels): bound draft-stream flush loop to prevent runaway sends
target.body:
## Summary

**Problem**: `createDraftStreamLoop().flush()` had a `while (!isStopped())` loop whose only exit was "no pending text after a send". A producer that keeps appending text between iterations keeps `pendingText` non-empty forever, so the loop never returns — the flush promise never settles, channel edit API calls fire back-to-back with no throttle, and the event-loop segment is starved (issue #106644).

**Solution**: bound each `flush()` invocation to at most `MAX_FLUSH_SENDS_PER_INVOCATION` (20) consecutive sends; on hitting the cap while text is still pending, hand the remainder back to the existing throttle timer via `schedule()` and return, yielding to the event loop without dropping the pending text.

**What changed**: added the `MAX_FLUSH_SENDS_PER_INVOCATION` bound plus reschedule in `flush()` (`src/channels/draft-stream-loop.ts`) and a regression test.

**What did NOT change**: throttle policy, channel adapters, and the controls layer are untouched; normal bursts stop replenishing and never reach the cap, so latency and existing behavior are unchanged.

Design note: preserving `pendingText` and rescheduling (rather than clearing it) is deliberate — clearing on the cap would silently drop the newest draft text. This matches the issue's "yield back to the main event loop" guidance.

Fixes #106644

---

## Root Cause

**Trigger condition**: `sendOrEditStreamMessage` keeps succeeding while new text is appended via `update()` between iterations, so `pendingText` is never empty when the loop checks `if (!pendingText) return`.

**Root cause analysis**: `flush()`'s while-loop lacked a per-invocation send bound. The throttle only gates `update()` -> `schedule()`, not the inner send loop, so a fast producer drives unbounded, un-throttled sends. Root: a missing loop boundary in `src/channels/draft-stream-loop.ts`.

**Affected scope**: channels using `createDraftStreamLoop` via `draft-stream-controls.ts` (streaming preview edits). `draft-stream-controls.ts` has no loop of its own and needs no change; its finalize paths mark the stream final before flushing, which blocks further `update()`, so the cap is never reached there.

---

## Linked context

- **Issue**: #106644
- **In scope**: per-invocation send bound plus reschedule in `flush()`; a regression test.
- **Out of scope**: throttle policy, channel adapters, and the controls layer.

---

## Real behavior proof

**Behavior addressed**: `flush()` no longer loops forever when pending draft text is continuously replenished; it terminates after a bounded batch and reschedules the remainder instead of blocking and hammering the channel edit API.

**Real environment tested**: Linux x86_64, Node v24.13.1, vitest v4.1.9; real process execution (not mocked) of the draft-stream-loop suite against the original vs patched source.

**Exact steps or command run after this patch**: run the suite against the unbounded original, then against the bounded patch.
```bash
# node vitest runs — Before fix (unbounded flush) then After fix (bounded flush)
git checkout HEAD~1 -- src/channels/draft-stream-loop.ts    # Before fix: remove the bound
timeout 60 node node_modules/.bin/vitest run src/channels/draft-stream-loop.test.ts --testTimeout=25000
git checkout HEAD -- src/channels/draft-stream-loop.ts      # After fix: restore the bound
node node_modules/.bin/vitest run src/channels/draft-stream-loop.test.ts --no-coverage
```

**After-fix evidence**:
```
Before fix (unbounded flush): the process never returns; it is killed by the
outer timeout. The microtask loop starves even vitest's own --testTimeout=25000,
so the runaway test cannot self-terminate:
    $ timeout 60 node ... vitest ... --testTimeout=25000
    exit 124     # process-level SIGTERM at 60s, test never completed

After fix (bounded flush):
    RUN  v4.1.9
    Test Files  1 passed (1)
         Tests  8 passed (8)
      Duration  1.10s
```

**Observed result after the fix**: the identical runaway scenario terminates in ~1s; before the patch it never completes and must be killed. The new test also asserts `takePending() === "text-21"`, proving the pending text is preserved (not dropped) when the cap engages.

**What was not tested**: a full live Telegram/Discord channel runaway (needs external channel accounts plus an adversarial rapid producer, unavailable in this environment); substituted by the real before/after suite execution above. Finalize paths are covered by `draft-stream-controls.test.ts` (12/12).

## Tests and validation

### Unit tests
```
$ node node_modules/.bin/vitest run src/channels/draft-stream-loop.test.ts --no-coverage
 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  8 passed (8)      # includes the new #106644 runaway regression test

$ node node_modules/.bin/vitest run src/channels/draft-stream-controls.test.ts --no-coverage
 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  12 passed (12)    # controls / finalize regression

$ node scripts/run-tsgo.mjs -p tsconfig.core.json --incremental ...   # exit 0 (typecheck)
$ node node_modules/.bin/oxlint src/channels/draft-stream-loop.ts src/channels/draft-stream-loop.test.ts   # exit 0 (lint)
```

## Risk checklist

merge-risk: Low

- [x] This change is backwards compatible
- [x] This change has been tested with existing configurations

target.title: fix(tts): allow trusted local media in message_tool_only mode

## Summary

Fixes openclaw/openclaw#83636.

Trusted local TTS media generated by tools can be dropped in `message_tool_only` room-event flows because the media was attached to message-tool source-reply transcript mirrors or consumed through suppressed block delivery before reaching the channel.

## The Fix

- Keep message-tool transcript mirrors immutable in `mergeAttemptToolMediaPayloads`.
- When trusted local tool media is present in `message_tool_only` mode, emit it as a standalone media-only payload instead of attaching it to the suppressed mirror payload.
- Route trusted per-block media payloads through delivery even when ordinary source delivery is suppressed.
- Run block TTS before suppression can drop eligible text blocks, then deliver trusted media as media-only.
- Strip private text from trusted block/final media before any `message_tool_only` bypass delivery.
- Keep ordinary final text, reasoning/status blocks, and untrusted media suppressed in ambient room-event contexts.
